articles.title: Romeo + Juliet at 30: how Baz Luhrmann made teens fall in love with Shakespeare
articles.text:
Romeo + Juliet is not the most renowned or beloved of Shakespeare’s plays, but it is perhaps the most foundational. The 16th-century tragedy, a story of love-addled teenagers and white-hot resentment, is often an English student’s first introduction to the bard’s oeuvre – more accessible and relatable to teens, with its plaintive lust and histrionic mood swings, than the more austere machinations in, say, Macbeth, Hamlet or Othello. And if Romeo + Juliet is the young person’s entry to Elizabethan English, perhaps no version of it is more worthy of the term “gateway drug” than Baz Luhrmann’s 1996 film version, which reimagined Verona’s family feud as a tropical gang war and launched an army of teenage crushes with the faces of Leonardo DiCaprio and Claire Danes.

The maximalist interpretation of Shakespeare’s most lovelorn work, released 30 years ago this week (!), retains Elizabethan verse but announces its divergence from rigid classicism from the jump. Our scene is set in fair Verona beach by a news anchor via TV set, relaying the woe of two star-cross’d lovers before clips of civil strife. Fresh off his breakout success in 1992’s Strictly Ballroom, the Australian director boldly mapped the medieval story on to 90s tabloid fixations – grainy footage of violence in the streets, magazine headlines of capos and criminals, helicopter views of car chases and riots that recalled the media circus around the OJ Simpson chase two years prior. It is a movie that could have only been made in the 90s; Luhrmann’s vision of two warring families as rival gangs, replete with their own economic operations and marked territory, tapped into the era’s preoccupation with gangland as a source of transportive art, from movies to hip-hop, and as a conservative fixation for ideas on intrinsic criminality.

Luhrmann and his wife, costume designer Catherine Martin, reimagined Verona as a sun-scorched beach city, incorporating real locations – Mexico City’s famed Immaculate Heart of Mary Church and Chapultepec Palace, Veracruz’s Boca del Río – to convey an urban den of simultaneous reverence and decay. The Montagues, with their heedless hollering and open Hawaiian shirts, and the Capulets, urban cowboys in Cuban-heeled boots, nearly vibrate with loathing and brandish guns marked by Catholic iconography. Perhaps compensating for the at times impenetrable verse, Luhrmann cut and spliced and twirled the camera in a frenetic, at times literal firework display of manic energy. The film’s raucous shootouts and parties now read as an obvious precursor to Euphoria high school – these kids dressed up and showed out, popped ecstasy and ripped around town in souped-up cars. Watching a single scene, even the lovers’ infamous fish tank meet-cute, has the feel of chugging an energy drink.

As such, the blatantly youth-aimed film had plenty of detractors in its time. Critics dismissed it as vulgar and garish, but audiences turned out en masse; Romeo + Juliet made over $147m against a $14.5m budget, boosted in part by a period-defining soundtrack with needle drops from The Cardigans, Everclear, Radiohead and Garbage. (And of course, the song from that oft-replayed fish tank scene, Des’ree’s I’m Kissing You, became the ubiquitous soundtrack for couple-shipping montage videos on 2000s YouTube). By the time I first viewed the film in 2009 – like many, in high school English class, as part of my teacher’s bid to get us invested in Shakespeare – it was already considered a classic.

That my teacher’s bid worked is largely due to the performances of the film’s two luminous stars, both brimming with the type of uncut, untameable desire known only to youth. Romeo + Juliet, of course, was a movie about teenage obsession that sparked a million teenage obsessions with DiCaprio (including from yours truly, who cried in English class not over the lovers’ double suicide – soooo melodramatic of them! – but over the realization that youth is fleeting and I would never be with anyone so beautiful. Devastating!) But it is a 17-year-old Danes, in a role originally intended for a text-accurate 13-year-old Natalie Portman (correctly deemed too childlike next to a 21-year-old DiCaprio), that shines on a rewatch. Her beauty is wide-open and uncomplicated, her face shaded with feelings as fresh and fleeting as morning dew. When her face falls, upon realizing her lover’s suicide, you feel, too, the ear-ringing fall of one’s first galling disappointment, the lurch of a sickening comedown.

That is the genius of Luhrmann’s Romeo + Juliet: it is a feelings-first movie, a portrait of teenage melodrama where all emotions exist only at full volume. That’s true for the highs – when the lip-locked lovers careen across a pool, or when Harold Perrineau’s Mercutio enters the scene with a high-kick in full silver drag to Kym Mazelle’s Young Hearts Run Free – as with the lows. In Luhrmann’s vision, Mercutio’s death at the hands of John Leguizamo’s Tybalt, a devilish sharpshooter with a soul patch, lands as equally tragic and torturous as the lovers. Perrineau stumbles, processes and curses both houses with such fervor as a real hurricane swept into Veracruz, that the rest of the film feels muted without him. And still, Romeo’s agonized poisoning, which frankly puts DiCaprio’s more famous death in the North Atlantic to shame, lands as a timeless gut-punch. So much youthful idealism and beauty, wasted on such petty grievances.

Luhrmann’s masterpiece more than transcended the more straightforward Shakespeare adaptations of the era, such as Kenneth Branagh’s Much Ado About Nothing (1993) and Hamlet (1996), Trevor Nunn’s Twelfth Night (1996) and Michael Hoffman’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream (1999). It arguably inspired the many modernizations kicked off by the runaway success of 1999’s 10 Things I Hate About You and continued by Easy A and She’s the Man. It quite evidently inspired a recent Broadway revival, starring Rachel Zegler and Kit Connor, that borrowed the Romeo + Juliet styling and the film’s stir-crazy bombast. But nothing has quite captured the imagination, or imparted the hot blood coursing in Shakespeare’s literary characters, like those two cursed houses in Verona beach. Thirty years on, we are still waiting for the next truly great, pop culture-shifting Shakespeare moment.

articles.title: Blue Planet III review – David Attenborough makes another absolute corker
articles.text:
We settle down in front of a fresh Blue Planet, trying to escape a weary sadness that stalks us from several angles. It is a new natural history show narrated by the 100-year-old David Attenborough, so there cannot be many more of those to enjoy. It is a Sunday-night showcase on BBC One, which is nothing like as significant a shared cultural event as it once was. The film-making can’t possibly be as revelatory as the original Blue Planet in 2001, and even the impact Blue Planet II had on conservation in 2017 feels unrepeatable: the attention it brought to plastic pollution in the ocean turned out to be a minor blow struck in a battle against environmental catastrophe that we have, since then, continued to lose.

But if we stop requiring it to be another landmark and appreciate it as just another wildlife series, Blue Planet III is a corker. Its excellence is a bright flash of hopeful defiance, and if it often falls into familiar patterns, that familiarity is a comfort.

There are, too, still wonders left to find. Episode one lands a scoop on the sandy sea floor in Shark Bay, Western Australia, where the Blue Planet team solve the mystery of why dolphins can be seen clutching sea sponges in their mouths. Stick around for the making-of featurette at the end, which reveals that solving the puzzle required the skilful use of the latest remote cameras, a careful courting of the dolphin in question, and the real risk of Alex, the cameraman, being eaten by a tiger shark.

Around the corner in northern Australia, tawny sharks are doing something new, or at least new to us: not just hunting in packs, but pulling off a grand deception as a team by pretending to be asleep so as not to spook the herring, before working together to drive those tasty minnows shorewards, trap them, and feast.

Every big new Attenborough show has to have a tense death chase, and for that we travel to Brazil, where it’s shark v turtle. The turtle loves to munch on seaweed at the bottom of the deeper waters away from the beach, but eventually it has to break the surface to grab some air, and by doing so it alerts the shark to its presence. A drone in the air above, and a camera fixed to a turtle’s back show us every play in the game as the turtle flees to the shallows and, when that doesn’t work, pulls off a sharp-turn manoeuvre that leaves the shark’s teeth glancing off hard shell.

We must, also, have some comic relief, to the sound of jauntier music and a playful mischief in Attenborough’s tone. So off we go to Indonesia, to marvel at a pair of harlequin shrimp in their ridiculous two-tone livery, tumbling around adorably as they try to snack on a starfish. Their every movement is funny, although it’s less amusing for the starfish, which suffers the indignity of having one of its arms pulled off by two prawns in jester costumes.

There’s more hilarity in the Brazilian mangroves, which brings us the obligatory report from the unnervingly relatable animal dating scene. In the sloppy mud of low tide, a fiddler crab is proud of his one big claw and waves it expectantly at the local females, only for the camera to pan back and reveal he is but one of hundreds of filthy loners, waggling their precious appendages and craving attention. We’ve all been there, son. The fiddler crab females, eyes on unbelievably cartoonish stalks that pop wryly up and fold dismissively back down, observe pitilessly as our friend is embroiled in a pincer-measuring contest with a rival, becomes fatally distracted, and is eaten by a passing scarlet ibis.

Still, it’s not all fun, and when Blue Planet III turns serious, it does so with stunning force. A lovely clownfish busily attends to the anemone it relies on for shelter, cleaning the tips of its tendrils and bringing it oxygenated water with a vigorous flapping of fins – but it’s doing that because a heatwave is killing the anemone, and the coral reef they both live on. As the destruction brought about by climate breakdown is illustrated with a horrific before/after edit – the sumptuous colours of the reef melting into dead blackish brown, in two shots filmed months apart – Attenborough makes the same plea he has delivered umpteen times before.

The delights we have been privileged to see are enough for us to wish, again, that this time he will be heard. “These tiny fish helped to protect their home,” the great man says, his voice these days weathered almost to a whisper. “Imagine what we could achieve if we all worked together to protect ours.”

articles.title: Juan Atkins, pioneer of Detroit techno sound, dies aged 64
articles.text:
Juan Atkins, one of the pioneers of Detroit techno and a huge influence on dance music more widely, has died aged 64.

His agency, Greensmith Artists, confirmed the news to the dance music website Resident Advisor, saying Atkins had been found unresponsive in a hotel room in Mexico City prior to a performance there, and was pronounced dead after being taken to hospital.

Atkins created a gleaming, mechanistic form of electronic music, first as part of the duo Cybotron and then under the alias Model 500, that could command a dancefloor while also evoking sci-fi fantasias. He was the first person to use the term “techno” in tandem with this hard electronic style, pre-empting an entire genre that now stands as one of the pillars of dance culture.

Born in Detroit in 1962, Atkins later moved with his family to the rural Michigan suburb of Belleville. “I just wasn’t used to going to school on a yellow bus and living on a dirt road,” he told the Guardian in 2024. But it was here that he met Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson, two junior high schoolmates with whom he formed the Belleville Three, a trio of like-minded musicians sitting at the vanguard of electronic music.

Still in high school and utilising increasingly affordable hardware such as the Roland TR-808 drum machine and the Korg MS-10 synthesiser, Atkins formed Cybotron with Richard Davis. “I had a class called future studies, about the transition from an industrial society to a technological society,” Atkins told the Guardian in 2014. “I just applied a lot of those principles to my music-making.”

Equally in thrall to Kraftwerk and Jimi Hendrix, Cybotron’s propulsive yet psychedelic tracks, such as Cosmic Cars and Clear, became dancefloor staples. The duo split​ in 1985, with Davis drawn more towards rock music. “I think that was where he wanted to be, in that album-orientated rock [scene],” Atkins later said.

Atkins went solo as Model 500, creating other foundational dance tracks such as No UFO’s and The Chase. In 1985, he also founded his own record label, Metroplex, to release his work. Over the years, it also put out material by artists including Anthony Shakir and DJ Bone.

Throughout​ the 1980s and beyond, Atkins evoked not just techno-utopian visions, but also more troubling and politicised ones. “I make social statements. My lyrics are supposed to make you think about something other than shaking your booty on the dancefloor and falling in love,” he told the Guardian in 2024.

By the early 1990s, the techno scene he helped inspire had flourished, and Atkins further finessed his sound with the uptempo project Infiniti later in the decade.

The 2000s were less productive in terms of releases, but he formed the duo Borderland with another techno icon, Moritz Von Oswald, releasing two albums in 2013 and 2016.

In 2023, Atkins reformed Cybotron, releasing new music and performing live. By this point, Atkins’s influence had extended far beyond techno, with dozens of artists sampling Clear alone. Missy Elliott made it the backbone of her track Lose Control, which reached No 3 on the US Billboard chart in 2005.

Saunderson was among those paying tribute to Atkins on Sunday, calling him “a true visionary who opened the door for so many of us, myself included”.

articles.title: Like many authors, I’m bombarded by scam fan mail. I wasn’t prepared for what would happen when I wrote back
articles.text:
There’s no humble way to say it: I get a lot of fan mail. Almost every day, multi-paragraph emails arrive from passionate and well-informed readers in Barcelona and Frankfurt, Chicago and Warsaw. They have appealing names like Bella Monroe, Thalina Rose and Tricia Claxton. Some of them are straightforward enthusiasts while others are more irreverent, like the one who signs off her messages “warm chaos”. Some love the “deadpan genius” of my novels while others admire my nonfiction’s “moral courage”. What they all have in common, though, is that they are entirely fake and trying to con me out of money. They promise to promote my work at their city-wide book clubs or spread the word among their reading communities, if only I transfer a few hundred dollars to cover costs.

In the age of generative AI, scam emails have achieved a new level of personalisation. Most writers I know are receiving a steady stream of emails like this. The messages are often sophisticated enough to bypass a spam filter and reach our inboxes, leaving us no option but to read them and ask the painful question: would any real, living person feel this strongly about my work? Or, as one writer friend put it, the reason I know they’re fake is because they’ve actually read all my books.

What makes it worse is that the AIs that help write these scams really have read all our books. Last year, Anthropic agreed to pay $1.5bn in compensation to the thousands of authors whose copyrighted work they’d used to train their AI, Claude. In July, a group of publishers filed a lawsuit against Google for utilising “one of the most prolific infringements of copyrighted materials in history” in order to train their AI, Gemini. So when writers receive these AI-assisted scam messages, we know we are being manipulated by a version of ourselves.

A few months ago, for example, I received a gushing email from Ottessa Moshfegh. The bestselling, Booker-shortlisted author of My Year of Rest and Relaxation – to my mind one of the most potent voices in contemporary fiction – was taking time away from producing her inimitable prose to write me a fan letter. I thanked her for getting in touch. We got chatting and I asked about her work-in-progress. She said that her new novel was “preoccupied with interior life: how emotions register, how they fail to, and what that absence or excess does to identity over time”. I thought we were making a real connection when she said that, really, the best way to understand her work was to explore her Amazon page. Sigh. Never meet your heroes. Other writers have received similar messages from fake Donna Tartt and fake Sally Rooney. It must be strange for the real Moshfegh, Rooney and Tartt to know that their novels have been harvested by tech corporations in order to create the ghost versions of themselves who now haunt the inboxes of their peers.

The correct response to all this is, of course, to simply report the email, block the sender and move on. But there is a part of me that fantasises about dramatically unmasking the scammer, revealing the villain beneath. So when I received an email from the founder of the Berlin Book Club, I decided to see how far I could get. I agreed that I did need help reaching new audiences. I was willing to pay for her connections and expertise. Soon we started discussing payment methods. She wanted me to use CashApp or make a direct bank transfer but I was insistent that I could only send hard cash. We went back and forth for a couple of days. I impressed on her that I had, at that very moment, 500 US dollars in crisp notes in an unmarked envelope and that I lived quite near the post office. She finally relented and gave me a physical address. Neither of us commented on how unusual it was for the founder of the Berlin Book Club to have a postal address in the Philippines. I went on Google Maps and was able to find the street in question, a rural two-lane road with palm trees, a junk shop, an evangelical church and a large building hidden behind high white walls.

The Philippines – along with Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia – is one of the countries most affected by organised crime networks running industrial-scale “scam farms”. Last year, authorities raided a facility in Bamban, north of Manila, freeing nearly 700 people who had been trapped there and forced to work as scammers. Inside the building, it resembled a hybrid between a call centre and a prison, rows upon rows of computers and green screens, and tiny dorms with bunk beds. About half of the workers were Filipino, while the others had been trafficked from China, Vietnam, Malaysia, Taiwan, Indonesia and Rwanda, their documentation withheld. The bosses, meanwhile, splashed around in the swimming pool next door. When another nearby compound was raided, they found it had its own brothel, karaoke suite and torture room. Across south-east Asia, these scam compounds are a multi-billion dollar industry, run largely by Chinese crime syndicates who routinely use violence and sexual abuse to keep workers in line. With the enormous sums of stolen money flowing through the industry, some compounds are the size of small towns or, perhaps more accurately, labour camps – with thousands of workers.

The scammers are encouraged to make use of the latest technology, not just generative AI but also face masking apps, so that they can conduct video calls wearing whatever face suits the task. The big focus is on “pig butchering”: long-term romance scams where people are tricked into falling in love with a wealthy, glamorous foreigner who then advises them to invest in fake cryptocurrency. When a large scam compound in Cambodia was seized by the Thai army, they discovered that its facilities resembled a TV studio. There were costumes, wigs and different sets for filming different scams. There was a fake Brazilian police station and a replica Vietnamese bank. Scammers were trained to keep their targets on the hook for months, even years, inventing private and personalised narrative worlds through which they could drain all of the victim’s money. In an interview with the BBC, one former scam compound manager sounded not unlike a novelist when he described the process. “[It’s] all about exploiting emotion,” he said. “You create a dream.”

For my part, I did not send any cash to the Philippines. Instead I shared the details I’d received with the country’s cybercrime agency. Although, in the words of Winston Casio, the spokesman for the presidential anti-organised crime commission in the Philippines, the ongoing problem is that the criminals have “the financial capability to corrupt just about anybody in public office. The amount of money they have is their potent tool against law enforcement.” When authorities shut down the Bamban compound, for example, they discovered that it was being run by Alice Guo, the local mayor. Similarly, the idea that AI companies might go out of their way to halt the criminal misuse of their technology seems just as doubtful – and for exactly the same reason. It’s making them fantastically rich.

All of which is to say that my fantasy of unmasking the villain was just that, a fantasy. At least now, when I receive fake fan mail, I can attempt to understand the probable reality behind the quirky name and upbeat tone. On the other side of the screen, there is someone frightened and far from home, sitting in a sound-insulated booth with a dozen phones splayed out on their desk – while behind them their manager walks by, a taser at his hip.
